key_insight: Tether uses correspondence-driven trajectory warping to repurpose prior trajectories into task-directed, on-policy experiences, enabling autonomous 'play' that produces diverse, functionally useful robot interactions and improves robustness to out-of-distribution states.
problem_solved: How to let robots autonomously generate useful, task-relevant experience (without heavy human demonstration) while maintaining a policy robust to diverse and out-of-distribution environment states.
method: Learn or compute correspondences between past trajectories/demonstrations and current environment states to identify how actions should transform under new conditions.
Apply trajectory warping to adapt and synthesize new, feasible action sequences that achieve the same functional goal in the current scene.
Run an autonomous play loop: execute warped trajectories to collect on-policy experience, then refine the policy with this continuously generated data for improved robustness and generalization.
impact: Enables scalable, less-supervised robotic learning by turning existing trajectories into a continual source of diverse, goal-directed experience—reducing reliance on manual demonstrations and improving real-world generalization.
visual_elements: Schematic of correspondence-driven warping: source trajectory mapped via correspondences to a new scene producing a warped trajectory.
Autonomous play loop diagram: warped trajectory → execution → data collection → policy update.
Before/after montage: original demo failure in an OOD state vs. successful warped execution in that state.
Performance schematic: qualitative bar or arrow showing improved robustness and data efficiency (no numeric claims, conceptual only).
paper_title: Tether: Autonomous Functional Play with Correspondence-Driven Trajectory Warping
paper_authors: William Liang, Sam Wang, Hung-Ju Wang, Osbert Bastani, Yecheng Jason Ma
